# Introduction {.unnumbered} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='minimal'} ## [Caution]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.10em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;'} This section is still being developed. The contents are subject to change. ::: :::: ## `ggplot2` syntax > “*making infinite use of finite means*” - Wilhelm von Humboldt Grammar is often defined as the system of rules for any given language and includes word meanings, internal structures, and word arrangement. Syntax is the form, structure and order for constructing statements. `ggplot2`'s syntax is built on the grammar & syntax of R. In R, objects are like nouns, and functions are like verbs (i.e., functions 'do things' to objects). The `ggplot2` syntax is comprised of layers, which we can use as templates to build increasing customize and complex graphs. ### The Data Layer The data layer consists of a rectangular object (like a spreadsheet) with columns and rows. Every dataset in this book is simulated, so we'll create one here: 150 home PCs sold in 1998, with each PC's `brand`, operating system (`os`), processor speed (`cpu_mhz`), and price (`price_usd`). Faster processors cost more, and Windows 98 adds a little to the price. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1998) pc_sales <- tibble( brand = sample(c("Compaq", "Dell", "Gateway"), 150, replace = TRUE), os = sample(c("Windows 95", "Windows 98"), 150, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.6)), cpu_mhz = sample(c(133, 166, 200, 233, 266, 300, 350, 400), 150, replace = TRUE), price_usd = round(700 + 4 * cpu_mhz + if_else(os == "Windows 98", 150, 0) + rnorm(150, 0, 200))) ggplot(data = pc_sales) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ### The Mapping Layer The mapping layer assigns columns (variables) from the data to a visual property (i.e. graph ’**`aes`**’ thetic) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=1920} ::: ::: **Basic Template**: Data, aesthetic mappings, geom ```r ggplot(data = ) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) ``` ### The Stats/Geoms Layer `geom_*()` functions include statistical transformations, shapes, and position adjustments for how to ‘draw’ the data on the graph ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) + geom_point( aes( shape = brand, color = os ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=1920} ::: ::: We can have multiple layers (data, mappings, geoms) in a single graph. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, # layer 1 mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) + geom_point( aes( shape = brand, color = os ) ) + # layer 2 geom_smooth( mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd), se = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=1920} ::: ::: - **Template + 1 Layer**: more geoms and more aesthetic mappings ``` r ggplot(data = ) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) ``` ### Position, Labels & Themes With a finite number of objects & functions, we can combine `ggplot2`’s grammar and syntax to create an infinite number of graphs! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = pc_sales, # layer 1 mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd ) ) + geom_point( aes( shape = brand, color = os ) ) + # layer 2 geom_smooth( mapping = aes( x = cpu_mhz, y = price_usd), se = FALSE ) + # layer 3 facet_wrap( . ~ brand, ncol = 2 ) + # labels labs( x = 'Processor speed (MHz)', y = 'Price (USD)', title = 'Home PCs in 1998', subtitle = 'Price vs. processor speed', caption = 'Simulated data' ) + # themes theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](intro_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=1920} ::: ::: **Template + 2 Layers + Facets + Theme + Labels** Layers = infinitely extensible! ```r ggplot(data = ) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) + geom_*(mapping = aes()) + facet_* + theme() + labs() ``` ## Graph Categories Graphs have been categorized into the following types (you can see them in the floating table of contents to your left). - **Univariate**: if you have a single column you're trying to visualize - **Amounts**: counts or simple summary statistics of one or two columns in a dataset - **Proportions**: ratio displays of part-to-whole - **Distributions**: displaying the shape of a variable's values (normalcy, skewness, kurtosis, etc.) - **Dates & Times**: changes in quantitative or categorical variables over a dimension of time (date-time, date, year, month, quarter, etc.). - **Relationships**: how does the change of values in variable `x` affect the values in variable `y` (and possibly `z`)? Some graphs can justifiably belong to more than one category, and wherever this is the case, I've tried to include links to other applications in the notes. ## Assumptions I've made an effort to write the graph code so it can be read and understood *without* having to execute it.[^intro-1] However, the examples assume the reader has already answered the question, “*what kind of data do I have?*”[^skimr-inspectdf] [^skimr-inspectdf]: If not, I highly recommend the [`skimr`](https://docs.ropensci.org/skimr/) and [`inspectdf`](https://alastairrushworth.github.io/inspectdf/) packages for getting to know your data better. ## Style & structure Each graph has the following sections: 1. **Prerequisites** - *Should I use this graph?*\ - *This graph requires:*\ 2. **Description** - *A brief summary of the graph's background, purpose, and aesthetics.* 3. **Set up** - Packages - *Code for installing development version of packages (if necessary) for graphs.* - Data - *The code that simulates the data for the graph (with `set.seed()`, so you get the same values every time).* 4. **Distribution** - *How the distribution we simulated from shapes the graph, in three steps:* - ***COUNT IT***: *look at a handful of values and a few summary numbers.* - ***DRAW IT***: *draw the data as a bar model or annotated graph.* - ***NAME IT***: *write down the distribution and connect each parameter to the graph.* 5. **The grammar** - Graph Code - *Graph labels have the `labs_` prefix* - *Graph layers have a `ggp2_` prefix* 6. **More info** - Additional methods, arguments, or applications - *Color palettes*\ - *Complimentary packages* The diagram below shows how the sections fit together. The data is simulated in **Set up**, explained in **Distribution**, and graphed in **The grammar**. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-cap: 'The sections in each graph chapter' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize': '14px', 'darkMode': false}}}%% flowchart TD req(["Prerequisites
what the graph needs"]) --> desc["Description
what the graph shows"] desc --> setup[/"Set up
packages + simulated data"/] setup --> dist subgraph dist["Distribution"] count["i. COUNT IT
values + summaries"] --> draw["ii. DRAW IT
bar model or
annotated graph"] draw --> name["iii. NAME IT
distribution +
parameters"] end dist --> grammar[["The grammar
labs_* + ggp2_*"]] grammar --> more(["More info
other geoms + options"]) style req fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style desc fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style setup fill:#C0C0C0,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style dist fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style count fill:#000080,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style draw fill:#000080,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style name fill:#000080,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style grammar fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style more fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 ``` I've attempted to balance brevity and clarity, but with the assumption that its best to err on the latter. I've also followed the general principle that if a graph can be *easily* built using one of `ggplot2` 's `geom_*` functions, that method is shown first. [^intro-1]: This field manual follows a [Rule of Least Power Principle](https://www.w3.org/2001/tag/doc/leastPower.html), in the sense that "*a language with a straightforward syntax may be easier to analyze than an otherwise equivalent one with more complex structure.*"
